historical_claims.anchor: In 1970, the economist Albert O. Hirschman published a book called *Exit, Voice, and Loyalty*.

historical_claims.source_locator: Book publisher summary: exit as switching/quitting
Book publisher summary: voice as influence from within

historical_claims.anchor: The Federal Communications Commission explains that people switching providers while remaining in the same geographic area can generally keep their number, including transfers among wireline, internet-protocol, and wireless services.
historical_claims.source_locator: FCC consumer guide: local number porting

historical_claims.anchor: The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, commonly called SMTP, specifies part of how mail systems hand messages to one another.
The British government's technology guidance makes a related point in its case for open standards.
historical_claims.source_locator: GOV.UK service manual, Working with open standards

historical_claims.anchor: Tim Berners-Lee, describing principles for the Web in the late 1990s, emphasized decentralization: designing systems so that essential operations do not depend on a single point of control.
historical_claims.source_locator: W3C Design Issues: Principles of Design (1998)

historical_claims.anchor: Article 20 of that regulation, adopted in 2016, provides a right in specified circumstances to receive certain personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and to transmit them to another controller without hindrance.

claim_evidence.anchor: Loyalty may preserve an opportunity for voice that would disappear if every dissatisfied person walked away immediately.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Hirschman contrasts loyalty supporting voice against exit undermining it.

claim_evidence.anchor: Portability does not make every transition effortless.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: FCC identifies fees and contract obligations as potential costs.

claim_evidence.anchor: A shared protocol is an agreement that a relationship between two people should not be completely determined by a relationship between two vendors.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: The normative implication is the author’s argument; interoperability as a technical mechanism comes from RFC.

claim_evidence.anchor: It explicitly identifies avoiding supplier lock-in, sharing data between services, and changing systems over time as reasons to use standards.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: GOV.UK includes all these motivations in its guidance.
GDPR limits right to specific bases and types of processing; not all data are in scope.

claim_evidence.anchor: A data file is not a friendship.
claim_evidence.evidence_detail: Discussion of collective dependence and limits of individual exit is original synthesis, not a literal quote from Hirschman.

authorship.scope: Original opinion essay. Historical and legal claims ground in publisher, government, and standard documentation. Constructed examples identified as such. Author does not claim private experiences or assert OpenAI positions.

background: No technical or legal prerequisites; introduces exit, voice, network effects, data portability, and interoperability with examples.
readiness_checks: Distinguish natural switching costs from restrictions designed to discourage exit.
Explain why Hirschman treats exit and voice as interacting rather than interchangeable responses.
Describe the value and the limits of telephone number portability.
Explain why SMTP interoperability does not mean every provider must guarantee delivery.
Describe why machine-readable export is not the same as a portable, editable project.
State why GDPR Article 20 is conditional, rather than a universal right to all data.
Describe how network effects can defeat individual portability without eliminating its value.
Identify the responsibilities of AI systems to leave users with usable independent artifacts.

description: Examines ownership and exit in digital systems, asking whether people can carry their work, records, and relationships when they leave a service.
